server.maintainedFrom: the Maintenance and Release Schedule of nextcloud/server

tools.label: ESLint
tools.why: nothing checks the frontend sources, so a wrong import is found by the build or not at all
tools.legacyWhy: ESLint 9 reads the flat config only; the eslintrc form, an .eslintrc file or the eslintConfig key in package.json, is ignored unless the run is pinned to ESLint 8

tools.label: Stylelint
tools.why: stylesheets are unchecked, and a mistake in CSS fails silently instead of loudly

tools.label: Psalm
tools.why: the PHP side has no static analysis, which is what catches a wrong type before the server does

tools.label: PHPUnit
tools.why: there is no test harness in the checkout, so nothing can be run against a change

tools.label: PHP-CS-Fixer
tools.why: no coding standard is applied to the PHP sources, so formatting is settled in review instead of by a command

tools.label: REUSE
tools.why: licensing is not machine-checkable, which the App Store and every distribution ask for

tools.label: EditorConfig
tools.why: indentation is whatever each contributor's editor does

lines: Version drift: appinfo/info.xml says 1.0.1, package-lock.json says 1.0.0, package-lock.json packages[""] says 1.0.0.

make version of ncmake bumps info.xml, composer.json and package.json and re-syncs package-lock.json in one step, so they cannot drift apart. ncmake's lint-version workflow fails a push or a pull request on exactly this drift. The App Store and the server read info.xml, npm and composer read their own manifest. Whichever is behind, a release ends up carrying more than one version number, and only one of them reaches the user.
appinfo/info.xml states no <repository>.
<repository> is the only machine-readable link from a published release back to the source it was built from. Without it nothing that reads the release can tell where its source is.
<website> is not set either.
Declares Nextcloud 29 to 31; the oldest maintained major is 33 (the Maintenance and Release Schedule of nextcloud/server), the newest released 35 (the release tags of nextcloud/server).
max-version 31 is below the oldest maintained major (33, the Maintenance and Release Schedule of nextcloud/server), so the release covers only servers that no longer receive fixes.
min-version 29 reaches below the oldest maintained major (33), which means the code has to keep working with APIs that are no longer tested upstream.
engines.node ^20.0.0 in package.json admits only end-of-life Node lines: the release is built on Node 20, which reached end of life on 2026-04-30.
That Node receives no security fixes, and the lockfile is resolved for it. The oldest line still maintained is Node 22.
Node release dates from schedule.json of nodejs/Release, as of 2026-11-13.
The app id is dashboardsearchbar, the checkout directory is nextcloud-dashboard-search-bar-app.

The server finds an app by its directory name, so the installed directory has to be named after the id. A checkout can be named anything, which is why this is a note and not a defect - but a tarball built from this directory name would not load.
A link of appinfo/info.xml has moved permanently:
<bugs> https://github.com/Jelmerovereem/nextcloud-search-engine-app/issues
now https://github.com/Jelmerovereem/nextcloud-dashboard-search-bar-app/issues
The old address works only as long as the redirect is kept; the new one can be stated directly.
PHP floor stated once: composer.json requires php ^8.1; appinfo/info.xml declares no php dependency.
Nothing contradicts anything here. Stating it in both places is what keeps a composer install from resolving packages for a PHP the server will not run.
Node 20 stated in main.yml, release.yml, within package.json engines.node ^20.0.0.
Not stated in .nvmrc, so nothing keeps the other places from drifting away from it.
package-lock.json (lockfileVersion 3) in the checkout.
composer.json without composer.lock.
An app ships its vendor tree, so the versions in it are part of the release; committing the lockfile is what makes that tree reproducible.
Tooling in the checkout: ESLint (eslint.config.mjs), Stylelint (stylelint.config.js), Psalm (psalm.xml).
No PHPUnit configuration: there is no test harness in the checkout, so nothing can be run against a change.
No PHP-CS-Fixer configuration: no coding standard is applied to the PHP sources, so formatting is settled in review instead of by a command.
No REUSE configuration: licensing is not machine-checkable, which the App Store and every distribution ask for.
No EditorConfig configuration: indentation is whatever each contributor's editor does.
package.json declares the script stylelint, which no installed workflow runs.
The template lint-stylelint of nextcloud/.github runs stylelint: make workflows-install W=lint-stylelint
A check that no workflow runs on a pull request catches only what the contributor who remembers to run it catches.
3 declared packages are named nowhere in the checkout: @nextcloud/initial-state, @nextcloud/eslint-config, @nextcloud/stylelint-config.

Searched as literal names over 26 files, package.json excluded apart from its non-dependency fields, lockfiles excluded; then as an ESLint shorthand, as what TypeScript takes from a tsconfig, and as a peer of an installed package in package-lock.json. A package loaded some other way is not named anywhere either, so this is a list to check, not a list to remove.
Licence mit (appinfo/info.xml), MIT (package.json, composer.json).
mit in appinfo/info.xml is a deprecated App Store value, shown there as MIT. An SPDX id there needs a <nextcloud> min-version of 31 or higher.
No LICENSES/ directory, so the licence text itself is not in the checkout, which is what REUSE and the distributions check for.
The ncmake bootstrap stub is in place (21 lines).
Every directory the shipped PHP reaches through __DIR__ and the frontend through linkTo is in the shipped file set.
